statements: The patient is a 73-year-old man.
His chief concern on presentation was 2 days of severe exertional, pressure-like chest pain.
His chest pain was rated 9/10.
The initial workup strongly supports an acute coronary syndrome.
His high-sensitivity troponin was markedly elevated at greater than 5000 ng/L.
His clinical presentation was consistent with ischemic chest pain.
His ECG showed normal sinus rhythm without ST elevation.
The presentation fits non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
He was appropriately started on heparin therapy.
He was appropriately started on antiplatelet therapy.
On hospital day 2, he developed new severe left lower abdominal pain.
On hospital day 2, he developed new severe thigh pain.
He developed the new left lower abdominal and thigh pain while receiving anticoagulation therapy.
He developed the new left lower abdominal and thigh pain while receiving antiplatelet therapy.
He had sudden severe pain in the left lower abdomen and thigh.
CT abdomen/pelvis showed marked swelling of the left psoas muscle.
CT abdomen/pelvis showed marked swelling of the left iliacus muscle.
CT abdomen/pelvis showed heterogeneous density consistent with hemorrhage.
CT angiogram showed active contrast extravasation into the left psoas muscle.
Angiography showed no arterial source of active bleeding.
The findings indicate a retroperitoneal intramuscular bleed centered in the iliopsoas compartment.
The absence of an arterial source on angiography makes a venous or small-vessel spontaneous bleed more likely than a major arterial injury.
The temporal relationship to heparin treatment is highly significant.
The temporal relationship to antiplatelet treatment is highly significant.
There is no mention of trauma.
There is no mention of falls.
There is no mention of an invasive femoral access complication.
There is no mention of an abdominal mass.
There is no mention of fever.
There is no mention of leukocytosis.
There is no mention of signs suggesting infection or abscess.
The physical exam at presentation was unremarkable.
Later imaging specifically described hemorrhage rather than another mass lesion.
The platelet count was 380 K/cm3.
The platelet count argues against thrombocytopenic bleeding.
The hemoglobin was initially 16 g/dL.
The hemoglobin later rose to 18 g/dL after stabilization.
A hemoglobin rise after stabilization is unusual for a major hemorrhage.
A hemoglobin rise after stabilization can occur with hemoconcentration.
A hemoglobin rise after stabilization does not negate the imaging-proven bleed.
The CTA finding of active extravasation confirms true hemorrhage.
The case includes anticoagulation-associated iliopsoas hematoma as a candidate differential.
Anticoagulation-associated iliopsoas hematoma fits best because of heparin and antiplatelet exposure and classic imaging findings.
Femoral-access or catheterization-related retroperitoneal bleed is a candidate differential.
No catheterization is described.
No femoral access is described.
The lack of catheterization or femoral access makes femoral-access related retroperitoneal bleed less likely.
Psoas abscess is a candidate differential.
Psoas abscess can cause psoas enlargement and pain.
The acute onset argues strongly against psoas abscess.
The heterogeneous hemorrhagic density argues strongly against psoas abscess.
Active contrast extravasation argues strongly against psoas abscess.
The lack of infectious features argues strongly against psoas abscess.
Spontaneous muscle infarction or diabetic myonecrosis is a candidate differential.
Spontaneous muscle infarction or diabetic myonecrosis can cause thigh pain in diabetics.
Imaging showed hemorrhage rather than infarction.
Imaging showed active extravasation rather than infarction.
Aortic or iliac vascular catastrophe is a candidate differential.
Angiography found no arterial source.
CT localized the process to intramuscular hemorrhage.
The most likely diagnosis is a spontaneous iliopsoas hematoma.
The iliopsoas hematoma is a retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
The iliopsoas hematoma was precipitated by anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy during NSTEMI treatment.
The diagnosis best explains the abrupt severe left lower abdominal and thigh pain.
The diagnosis best explains the CT evidence of psoas and iliacus hemorrhage.
The diagnosis best explains the CTA extravasation.
The diagnosis best explains the need to stop antithrombotic therapy.
The final diagnosis is anticoagulation-associated iliopsoas hematoma.
